# Character-Level Language Model
 
This is a project made purely for a better understanding of core concepts. I followed Andrej Karpathy's *Makemore* series in order to build up to this. The project only uses lowercase words (no capital letters).
 
## What Does It Do
 
It is trained on a set of ~30K random names for the sole purpose of producing more name-sounding words — which might be useless, but is pretty cool.

### Some names generated by the model
- zayce
- elleya
- jasley
- xenneth
- darceline

These are totally new words produced by the trained model, these can't be found in the training dataset.

### Classification of letters
If you drop the size of the embedding vectors to 2, and plot the resultant scatter plot for each letter, you can see the classification between vowels and consonants

<img width="690" height="523" alt="image" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e14ad583-b45a-43ef-9e42-f38b7aff5922" />

Even though the classification isn't really very clean but the mere fact that all the vowels are on one side and the consonants are huddled up in the center, impressed me. You can also see the `.` character being isolated. 

#### Note
This kind of clear classification was only produced when using Batch gradient descent with constant learn rate of 0.1.

## Dataset
 
A notepad file with ~30K names has been uploaded to this repo.

- emma
- olivia
- ava
- isabella
- sophia
- charlotte
- mia
- amelia
- harper
- evelyn

These are the first ten words.
 
## Hyperparameters
 
| Parameter            | Value    |
|-----------------------|----------|
| Iterations             | 50K – 100K |
| Batch size              | 64       |
| Learning optimizer     | AdaGrad  |
| Learning rate            | 0.01     |
| Number of hidden layers | 4        |
| Context size             | 10       |
| Embedding size           | 10       |
| Hidden layer size        | 300      |
 
## Structure
 
- **Embedding layer** — Converts each character to its specific embedding using the embedding matrix.
- **Flatten layer** — Flattens the embeddings into a 1-dimensional vector of size `context_size × embedding_size` (100 in this case).
- **Linear layer** — 100 neurons, ReLU activation.
- **Hidden layers** — All hidden layers have 300 neurons with a Tanh activation function.
- **Final layer** — 27 output neurons, representing weights for the 27 possible characters.

## Explanation
 
### Defining the Vocabulary
 
The vocabulary consists of all letters of the English alphabet plus a `.` character, which signifies the end of a word.
 
### Getting Input–Output Examples for Training
 
In supervised learning, we need inputs and desired outputs to train the model.
 
To get this kind of data from plain words, we use substrings of a word as inputs, and the next letter after each substring as the corresponding output.
 
#### Example
 
Take the word **"emily"**, with a context window of 3:
 
| Input sequence | Output |
|-----------------|--------|
| `[. . .]`       | `e`    |
| `[. . e]`       | `m`    |
| `[. e m]`       | `i`    |
| `[e m i]`       | `l`    |
| `[m i l]`       | `y`    |
| `[i l y]`       | `.`    |
 
The `.` output represents the end of the word. This single word produces 6 input–output pairs. Repeating this process across the dataset produces many such pairs, which are used to train the network.
 
Note that different words will produce different outputs for the same input sequence (e.g. `[. . .]`). This is expected — the output is essentially a probability distribution. For example, if there are roughly equal numbers of names starting with each letter, the output for `[. . .]` would give almost equal probability to all 26 letters and a tiny probability to `.` (since empty strings don't occur).
 
### Encoding and Embedding
 
Once the input–output pairs are prepared, letters are converted into numbers:
 
- Letters `a`–`z` are encoded as `1`–`26`.
- The `.` character is encoded as `0`.
Each encoding indexes a row in the embedding matrix (27 × 10 in this case), and the concatenated vector of these embeddings forms the network's input.
 
The network then performs its usual operations and produces the output distribution.
 
### Generating Words
 
To generate a word, the model is given the initial sequence of `.` characters as input. The next character is sampled from the resulting output distribution (a multinomial distribution over 27 characters).
 
This process repeats in a loop, feeding each new character back into the context, until the predicted character is `.` — at which point the loop ends and the completed word is added to the output list.
 
This procedure shows some degree of "memory" as about 26% of generated words already exist in the original dataset. Models with less memorization are possible, but word quality tends to degrade as memorization decreases. There seems to be a sweet spot between memorization and genuine novelty in the generated words.
 
### A Catch
 
I initially tried using batch normalization to avoid manually multiplying in Kaiming gains for each layer. However, batch norm ended up producing noticeably worse words overall (despite a lower memorization percentage).

### How learning looks

Well, most of the noise in the training loss is pretty much because of the batch size. But we can see the validation loss stabilizes pretty quickly.
